accepted.question_text: Given a polynomial Diophantine equation P(x1, ..., xn) = 0 with integer coefficients, determine whether its set of integer solutions is a finite union of polynomial families, where a polynomial family means a subset S of Z^n for which there exist polynomials P1, ..., Pn in integer parameters u1, ..., uk such that (x1, ..., xn) belongs to S exactly when xi = Pi(u1, ..., uk) for all i.

evidence.quote: Definition 1. Let Zn be the set of vectors (x1, . . . , xn) with integer coordinates xi. We say that a subset S subseteq Zn is a polynomial family if there exist an integer k >= 0 and polynomials P1, . . . , Pn in k variables u1, . . . , uk with integer coefficients such that (x1, . . . , xn) in S if and only if there exist integers u1, . . . , uk such that xi = Pi(u1, . . . , uk), i = 1, . . . , n.
Problem 1. Given a polynomial Diophantine equation (1), determine whether the set of its integer solutions is a finite unions of polynomial families.

accepted.question_text: Find a complete and mathematically usable description of all integer solutions to the Diophantine equations y^2 + z^2 = x^3 + 1 and y^2 + z^2 = x^3 - 1.
accepted.context_brief: Integer solutions for two cubic-sum equations

evidence.quote: Given a polynomial Diophantine equation (1), one may ask whether its set of integer solutions can be described in any "reasonable" way.
Nevertheless, the smallest equations for which we currently do not know a "satisfiable" answer are the equations y^2 + z^2 = x^3 + 1 (3) and y^2 + z^2 = x^3 - 1. (4)

accepted.question_text: Find explicit parametrizations or another complete description of all rational solutions to the Diophantine equations y^2 + z^2 = x^3 + 1, y^2 + z^2 = x^3 - 1, and y^2 - x^2 y + z^2 + 1 = 0.
accepted.context_brief: Rational solutions for smallest open examples

evidence.quote: If we ask the same question about rational solutions, then the smallest open are the same equations (3) and (4), as well as the equation y^2 - x^2y + z^2 + 1 = 0 (5).
We know that the corresponding cubic surfaces are unirational, see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/452461/, but currently do not know explicit parametrizations.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether the integer solution set of x^2 y + y^2 z + z^2 x = 1 is finite or infinite.

evidence.quote: The smallest open non-symmetric cyclic equation is x^2y + y^2z + z^2x = 1 (9) of size H = 25.
For this equation, we even do not know whether its integer solution set is finite or infinite.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether the Diophantine equation x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 2 has infinitely many integer solutions that are not permutations of (x, y, z) = (1 - 6t^3, -6t^2, 1 + 6t^3) for integers t.
accepted.context_brief: Open symmetric equation x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 2

evidence.quote: The smallest open symmetric equation is either x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 1 (10) of size H = 25 or x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 2 (11) of size H = 26, depending on whether you are satisfied with the description of integer solutions to (10) presented in [1, Section 4.4.1].
Equation (11) is open without any doubts, because we do not even know whether it has infinitely many integer solutions that are not permutations of (x, y, z) = (1 - 6t^3, -6t^2, 1 + 6t^3), t in Z.

accepted.question_text: Besides the obvious solutions already known, determine whether the Diophantine equations x^3 y + y z^2 + z = 0 and x + x^3 y + y z^2 = 0 have any other integer solutions.
accepted.context_brief: Three-monomial equations with unknown extra solutions

evidence.quote: The smallest open three-monomial equations are (a) x^3y + yz^2 + z = 0, (b) x + x^2y^2 + z^3 = 0 (13) and x + x^3y + yz^2 = 0. (14)
Equations (13) and (14) are open without any doubts, because they have some obvious solutions, see [1, Section 4.3.5], and it is open whether they have any other solutions.

accepted.question_text: Given a Diophantine equation P(x1, ..., xn) = 0, determine whether for every integer k >= 0 there exists an integer solution (x1, ..., xn) such that min(|x1|, ..., |xn|) >= k; if such arbitrarily large solutions do not exist, describe all integer solutions.

evidence.quote: Problem 2. Given a Diophantine equation (1), determine whether for any k >= 0 it has a solution such that min(|x1|, . . . , |xn|) >= k.
If yes, the problem is solved. If not, then describe all its integer solutions.

trace.notes: Mapped an 11-page paper titled 'A systematic approach to Diophantine equations: open problems'. Major open-problem regions are Sections 2 through 7, with explicit numbered Problems 1 through 7 and additional concrete equation-level open cases on pages 2-9.
Section 2 yields Problem 1 plus concrete open cases about describing all integer or rational solutions, including equations (3), (4), (5), (9), (11), (13), and (14).
Section 4 yields explicit Problem 2 and Problem 3, along with table-based concrete instances that remain open.
Section 5 yields explicit Problem 4 plus concrete open instances such as x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 3 and other table-based cases.
Section 6 yields explicit Problem 6 and concrete open existence questions from Tables 10-12.
Section 7 yields shortest-open summaries, including ambiguous cases for equation (38) and a concrete shortest open cubic existence problem (39).

Moved equations (12) to needs_review because the paper explicitly says their openness status is debatable, so the candidate fails the unambiguous-status gate.
